I have been farming these 16 mu for 45 years. I never went to school, but I know every inch of this land. My wife and I are getting old — just the two of us now — so we keep to what we know works. Everyone around here grows wheat in winter and maize in summer. I have done it my whole life.

For wheat, I will rotary till the land in early October, just like always. I will sow improved wheat seed — the kind they sell at the shop, what my neighbors use. I put down about one bag of compound fertilizer per mu, and then top up with urea. Last year I used a bit less and the wheat looked yellow, so this year I will stick to my usual amount — roughly 15 kg of nitrogen worth per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium from the compound bag. I have a well, so I will irrigate three times: once after sowing, once when the wheat is jointing, and once at grain filling. I also spray four times — herbicide once, insecticide twice, and fungicide once if I see rust on the leaves. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 850 jin per mu.

For maize, there is no time to waste after wheat harvest in early June. I plant hybrid maize seed — Denghai 605, same as my nephew uses — and I do it no-till. The soil is still loose from the wheat rotary tillage, and I am too old to till twice in one week. I spread a bit less fertilizer on the maize than the wheat — about 12 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium. Two irrigations are enough for maize: one right after planting if June is dry, and one when the cobs are filling. I spray three times — herbicide once and insecticide twice. The maize usually gives me around 1000 jin per mu if the rain does not fail.

I do not change much from year to year. Change is risky when you are 65 and have no pension. I would rather spend a little more on fertilizer than risk a bad harvest.
